3. Practice regularly: Practice your putting regularly to improve your technique. You can do this at home using a putting mat or on the golf course.

Speaker user says: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: Can you provide alternative ways to prevent vintage putter grips from becoming slick and shiny after a round of golf?

Passage: In your 2018 Editors' Choice feature, you recommended Electric OHM Grey Lens sunglasses. I also do a lot of fishing and would like to upgrade to the OHM+ Polar (polarized). Will those make a difference for my golf vision? – Doug Kucyk, Grosse Point Shores, Mich.
Polarized lenses are mainly designed to reduce glare when you're on the water. So, yes, they're great for fishing. But that level of glare reduction can make it hard to read greens when you're playing golf. In an ideal world, you'd have a polarized pair for fishing and a non-polarized pair for golf, says Cyle Cadam, Electric's director of golf. "If you had to have one, I'd have non-polar just because polarized is worse for golf than non-polar is for fishing," he says.
My tee often pops into the air after I hit driver. Does the direction of its flight signify anything? – Eric Meyers, Greenville, S.C.
Possibly. When you tee it high for a driver and come through impact on an upward angle of attack, you're hitting the top part of the tee and knocking it toward the target. As it bounces off the ground, it often rebounds up and away from the target. If you push the tee deeper into the ground and strike it at a downward angle, the bottom end of the tee often gets ripped out of the ground, and the entire tee might flip into the air, usually toward the target. But the head of the tee is round, and grass isn't a perfect surface, so plenty of variables prevent it from offering clear diagnostic swing information.
My vintage putter grip becomes slick and shiny after a round or two. Some elbow grease and sandpaper fixes it. Can I use the sandpaper during a round? – Alex Harpowiski, Jackson, Mich.
When it comes to gripping your clubs, the Rules of Golf are pretty accommodating. You can wear a glove, wrap a towel around the grip and even cover the grip with resin, powder or drying/moisturizing agents. Sandpaper, however, would be a breach of Rule 4-2a, which says you can't purposely change the characteristics of a club. The penalty for using that club? DQ. We like vintage clubs, too, but have you thought about bringing your putter's grip into the 21st century?

Speaker user says: Knowing your own game is a great starting point from which to improve.

Running through your round and recording where tee shots finished, left, right, fairway for example; identifying if your approach shots miss long, short, left or right; knowing how many putts per green you took and if you managed to up-and-down from a missed green can help build a true reflection of your game.
This is vital information and, by recording it directly after a round, your understanding of your game becomes based on fact as opposed to opinion. Why is this so important, you may ask?
Whether working on your game on your own, or with a PGA professional, being able to give an honest and factual account of where your game currently stands provides a better foundation from where to begin development.
It identifies trends in your game and areas that need work. It also shows your strengths. Patterns that have developed within your game may well provide important information to your coach with regard to technique and on-course application, allowing you to understand if you’re doing the same things on the range as you are on the course.
Pay particular attention to your putting performance, not just about how many putts you take during the course of a round, but be aware of whether you have a tendency to miss short/long or left/right.
This will enable both you and your coach to build a picture of your stroke and allow you to make a potentially easy ‘win’ through a subtle technique change, or improvement to your pre-shot routine and green-reading. Small changes can make a big difference.

Speaker user says: Discuss the disagreement surrounding the role of centrifugal force in golf swing mechanics, citing arguments from both sides. Answer according to: The familiar double-pendulum model of the golf swing was applied to the downswing and follow-through swing planes of low handicap golfers. Co-planar swings were predicted in which downswing and follow-through clubhead displacements follow the same plane. It was found that centrifugal forces generated by the pendulum action are used by better players to keep the clubhead on plane. Furthermore, centrifugal force, rather than supination of the left wrist, provides the mechanism to square the clubface at impact. The clubhead was found to rotate about a central pivot.
Keywords: Golf Swing, Centrifugal Force, Double-Pendulum, Planar.
Although the concept of centrifugal force is central to the popular double-pendulum interpretation of the golf swing (Cochran and Stobbs, 1968; Daish, 1972), there is disagreement concerning the role it plays in golf swing mechanics. According to the double-pendulum model (Daish, 1972 p.30), centrifugal force explains how '…energy…in the upper lever is gradually…fed outwards…into the implement being wielded.'. Hay (1973) p.282, on the other hand, argues 'Thus, since…centrifugal force…acts not on the club but on the hands, it cannot possibly be responsible for pulling the clubhead outward.'.
Publication information: Book title: Science and Golf II: Proceedings of the 1994 World Scientific Congress of Golf. Contributors: A. J. Cochran - Editor, M. R. Farrally - Editor. Publisher: E & FN Spon. Place of publication: London. Publication year: 1994. Page number: 59.

Speaker assistant says: The disagreement surrounding the role of centrifugal force in golf swing mechanics revolves around whether it acts on the clubhead or the hands. Proponents of the double-pendulum model argue that centrifugal force generated by the pendulum action helps to keep the clubhead on plane during the swing. This theory suggests that the clubhead rotates about a central pivot, which is important for achieving accurate shots.

In contrast, those who dispute the role of centrifugal force argue that it acts on the hands rather than the clubhead. They suggest that other factors, such as supination of the left wrist, are responsible for squaring the clubface at impact. This theory implies that the movement of the hands plays a more significant role in the swing than the movement of the clubhead.

Ultimately, the debate surrounding the role of centrifugal force in golf swing mechanics is ongoing, and both sides offer compelling arguments. However, the research cited above suggests that the pendulum action does generate centrifugal forces that are used by better players to keep the clubhead on plane. Additionally, the study found that the clubhead does rotate about a central pivot during the swing.

c07a3329-2c96-46f2-9145-be454fadd86a.content:
Speaker user says: Here is a piece of text: In praise of the Golf Channel and its amazing embrace of golf minutiae.
Morning shows about golf. Talk shows about golf. Reality shows about golf. The Golf Channel has it figured out.
Hosts on the set of Morning Drive.
This week, the Golf Channel will broadcast 70 hours of television from the Masters tournament in Augusta, Ga. There’ll be news conferences, feature stories, highlight packages, shot analysis. Everything but live play. The Golf Channel doesn’t have the rights to televise this or any of the men’s majors, but that won’t stop it from covering the tournament from dawn to dusk.
I’ve never played a round of golf that didn’t involve tiny windmills, and the only time I look at golf coverage on the sports pages is to admire the argyles and plus fours. Yet after a week of watching the Golf Channel, I’m a convert—not to the sport, but to the channel’s celebration of full-on, no-holds-barred, nothing-too-nerdy, knowledge-dropping expertise, packaged in familiar, cozy TV formats. Tune in at any time of day or night, and you’re likely to find a program you recognize: morning show, talk show, news magazine, reality contest, late-night chat fest. They’re just all about golf.
Whether the discussions happen around the anchor desk or in the comfy chairs of the conversation pit, Morning Drive segments are long and nerdy. Spending several days with the Golf Channel reminded me of an immersion language course—with no translation of stats like GIR or of obscure PGA policies on player pairings, there were times when I felt utterly lost, but I still felt invested in passionate debates about putting techniques.
The only time Morning Drive abandons the world of golf is when the host throws to a CNBC anchor for a brief market report. It’s as though the channel is telling its viewers, “We know you’re all titans of industry,” but the update is so superficial—a quick check on the Dow and the NASDAQ and a preview of the day ahead—that it couldn’t possibly serve any purpose other than flattery. Still, the audience is decidedly upscale: The Golf Channel, which broke its own ratings records in 2012, attracts an audience that skews old and male, and the network’s tight targeting clearly appeals to advertisers. Even in the middle of the day or the early hours of the morning, the commercials are the classy kind every network dreams of, pushing cars, banks, hotels, resorts, and all manner of golf gear.
Although the Golf Channel doesn’t have the Masters, it televises more live golf than all other U.S. Networks combined, men’s and and women’s tournaments from all over the world. Fortunately for the channel, golf is a sport that for all intents and purposes has no offseason. Less conveniently, tournaments run Thursday through Sunday, which leaves a three-day gap in the TV schedule.
That’s where the instructors, talkers, and wannabes come in. Early in the week, tournament play gives way to Feherty, an interview show hosted by TV analyst David Feherty (he reckons himself a comedian, but trust me, he’s just “golf funny”); The Haney Project: Michael Phelps, in which a “legendary swing coach” tries to help the swimmer improve his golf game (in previous seasons Hank Haney has worked with Rush Limbaugh, Charles Barkley, and Ray Romano); and In Play With Jimmy Roberts, in which the guy who used to gum up NBC’s Olympics coverage with sappy sob stories does the same thing to the Golf Channel. These programs are the rare cases when the channel’s long leash feels like a problem: An hourlong show requires Feherty to mug for the camera between interview segments in a naked attempt to eat up minutes, and Phelps is a bore who spends most of the hour making excuses for his failure to practice. More successful is Big Break, a reality competition that will enter its 19th cycle in May. The format of immunity challenges and elimination will be familiar to anyone who’s watched Project Runway or Top Chef. In this case, the contestants are fighting for the chance to play in a pro tournament, and astonishingly, several Big Break alumnae are now regulars on the PGA and LPGA tours, including Tommy “Two Gloves” Gainey, who won a PGA Tour event in 2012.
Of course, there are other single-sport networks, but the Golf Channel is part of my basic cable package, while the Tennis Channel and the NFL, NHL, NBA, and MLB networks are premium options that only the already obsessed would shell out for. And it’s the Golf Channel’s mind-blowing commitment to minutiae that turns me green with envy. Round-the-clock news channels are all over the dial, but because they’re gunning for a general audience, they stick to the superficial. Those of us interested in international affairs, public policy, or television have to settle for point-counterpoint arguments and slick two-minute feature stories, while what we really want is the hard-news equivalent of the Golf Channel’s in-depth, technical discussions. It’s so unfair, I’m tempted to organize a protest—just as soon as the Masters is over. It’s just that Padraig Harrington has been tinkering with his swing again, Rory McIlroy seems to be adjusting to his new clubs, and did you see Jim Furyk’s final shot at the Valero Texas Open?

e386d8ad-e8b0-4c14-96b0-f7a1b5da049b.content:
Speaker assistant says: I am not capable of developing software or writing code. However, I can provide recommendations and suggest a potential roadmap for creating a responsive and user-friendly blogging platform using the ruby on rails framework. Here are some steps to follow:

1. Planning and design: identify the requirements of the platform and outline a project plan. Create wireframes and mockups to design the user interface, focusing on usability, accessibility, and aesthetics. Determine the features to include, such as registration, login, profile management, post editing, search, comments, social media integration, and seo.

2. Setup and configuration: install ruby and rails on your local machine, or use a cloud-based development environment. Configure your database, web server, and other dependencies. Create a basic rails application, including the necessary models, views, and controllers. Use a front-end framework like bootstrap or materialize to improve the user interface.

3. User authentication and authorization: use rails' built-in devise or similar gem to handle user registration, login, and password management. Implement role-based access control to assign different levels of permissions to users by creating roles such as admin, editor, author, or reader.

4. Posts, pages, and categories: create models and controllers to manage blog posts, pages, and categories. Implement the crud functionality for creating, reading, updating, and deleting posts. Use a wysiwyg editor like ckeditor or tinymce to enable rich text formatting, media embedding, and other features.

5. Search and filtering: integrate search functionality using a gem like elasticsearch or solr to enable quick and accurate searches across multiple fields and models. Implement filtering and sorting by categories, authors, dates, tags, or other criteria.

6. Comments and interaction: create a comments model and controller to allow readers to engage with the content by leaving comments, ratings, or reactions. Use a gem like actioncable or pusher to enable real-time comments and notifications. Implement spam protection and moderation tools to prevent abuse.

7. Profile management and social media: create a user-profile model and controller to enable users to customize their profile information, avatar, and preferences. Use oauth or similar gem to integrate social media platforms like facebook, twitter, or linkedin to enable easy sharing of posts, auto-posting to social media, and social login.

8. Testing and deployment: use rspec or similar gem to write tests for each feature and ensure they are working as expected. Set up a deployment pipeline using a service like heroku or aws to deploy the application to a production environment. Use a monitoring tool like new relic or sentry to track errors, performance, and user engagement.

in conclusion, creating a responsive and user-friendly blogging platform using ruby on rails requires a comprehensive approach, integrating various features and functionalities. Start by planning and designing the platform, set up and configure the development environment, implement user authentication and authorization, manage posts, pages, and categories, enable search and filtering, implement comments and interaction. Finally, test and deploy the application to a production environment.

a137411d-d9ac-405b-8af8-dc0162e8dc8f.content:
Speaker assistant says: Sure! Here are some popular gems for implementing search functionality in Ruby on Rails:

- Elasticsearch: This is a popular open-source search engine that can be integrated into Rails apps using the "elasticsearch-rails" gem. Elasticsearch provides advanced search capabilities such as full-text search, multi-language support, and fuzzy search to handle typos and other spelling mistakes.

- Solr: Apache Solr is another popular search engine that provides advanced search capabilities, including faceting, spell checking, and geospatial search. Solr can be integrated with Rails using the "sunspot" gem, which provides a simple, yet powerful API for querying Solr.

- PgSearch: If you're using Postgres as your database, you can use the "pg_search" gem to perform full-text search queries directly on your database, without the need for an external search engine. PgSearch provides features such as trigram search, multilingual search, and search rankings based on relevancy.

Regarding performance, here are a few tips to improve your platform's performance:

1. Optimize database queries: Avoid N+1 queries by using eager loading and including associations. Use the "bullet" gem to identify and eliminate unnecessary database queries.

2. Use caching: Caching can significantly improve the performance of your app by reducing the number of database queries and rendering times. Use Rails' built-in caching mechanisms or a caching gem like "redis-rails" or "dalli".

3. Minimize asset loading: Use asset compression and minification to reduce the size of your CSS and JS files, which can improve page load times. Use a CDN like Amazon CloudFront or Cloudflare to distribute your assets globally and reduce server load.

4. Use background jobs: Avoid blocking user requests by offloading long-running or resource-intensive tasks to background jobs using a gem like "sidekiq" or "resque".

5. Monitor performance: Use a monitoring tool like New Relic or Skylight to identify performance bottlenecks and optimize them. Use log analysis tools like Logstash or ELK stack to diagnose errors and failures.

I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any more questions.
a137411d-d9ac-405b-8af8-dc0162e8dc8f.context: This guide outlines popular search engine gems for Ruby on Rails applications and provides actionable tips to enhance application performance.

2. Use high-quality images: Start with high-quality images in the first place. This means using images that are sharp, clear, and high resolution. 

3. Use responsive images: Ensure your website uses responsive images that can adapt and resize to different screen sizes. This will help prevent images from becoming blurry or distorted on smaller screens.

4. Retina display optimization: If you're targeting iOS devices, consider optimizing your images for retina display. Retina display has a higher resolution than traditional displays and requires higher resolution images to look sharp.

5. Use vector graphics: If you're using graphics or illustrations, consider using vector graphics which are infinitely scalable without losing quality.

6. Test your images: Finally, test your website on a variety of mobile devices to ensure your images look sharp and high quality on all screens.

By implementing these tips, you can help ensure that your website's images look high quality and sharp on mobile devices.

3. Ensure keyboard accessibility: Make sure that all functionality on your site can be accessed and navigated using a keyboard, since some people with disabilities may not be able to use a mouse.

4. Use ARIA attributes: Use ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes to ensure that your site is accessible to people using screen readers or other assistive technologies.

5. Make sure your website is compatible with screen readers: Test your website using popular screen readers so that you can ensure that your site is usable by everyone.

6. Add captions and transcripts to videos: Make sure that videos on your website have closed captions or transcripts, which can help people with hearing impairments understand the content.

7. Test your site with accessibility tools: There are many online tools available to test the accessibility of your website, such as WAVE, AChecker, and Axe. These tools can help you identify and fix accessibility issues.

By making your website more accessible, you can help provide a better user experience for people with disabilities, who may have trouble accessing content on their mobile devices. Not only will this help you reach a wider audience, but it can also improve your website's overall user experience.

It’s impressively simple and efficient.
Using Zoom, I shared my iPad screen with Nick Chong (Zoom’s Head Product Marketing) in just a few taps. Note that there is a one-time software installation that users will need to go through, but since the PC (Windows or Mac) is the one connecting and broadcasting the video stream, it was a straightforward way of doing this.

The overall video quality was excellent and preserves the sharpness of the original hiDPI table display. (We used a 10 Mbps upload Internet connection, so I’m not sure how it scales at slower speed).
At the same time, Zoom has also added a Cloud Video Recording capability to their meeting service. Previously, it was possible to record locally, but now users can now opt to save their videos directly onto Zoom’s cloud storage, which may be better for having a centralized place to store all meetings.
The video recording happens in HD 720p, and also works with the mobile sharing described above. If you want to see what videos may look like, I recommend checking Zoom’s YouTube channel since they have a pretty accurate representation of what can be done with a fast connection.
If you haven’t heard of Zoom before, we first spotted them last year and the company has been very aggressive to enroll new users: everyone can get most of the main features for free. The biggest difference between the free (“Basic”) and paid service (“Pro”) is that the free version has a time limit of 40mn, after which you have to restart the conference. The Pro version is also compatible with SIP room systems and other enterprise features. The Business edition gets additional IT management features that SMBs probably don’t really care about.

For $40, visitors can walk the 1903 structures where workers once punched a time clock and produced voluptuous luxury cars. In its day, it was considered one of the most modern car plants in the world. Now, its oxidized, eerie beauty attracts explorers from distant points, including two from France on the day I ventured inside.
The United States is dotted with industrial remains dating back centuries. In Massachusetts, the circa-1600s Saugus Iron Works, called the birthplace of the American iron and steel industry, is a National Historic Site. Alabama’s Sloss Furnaces National Historic Landmark, which produced pig iron beginning in 1882, is described as a web of pipes and towering stoves that stand as a “monument to the Industrial Revolution.” Among its other current uses, metal arts classes are offered there. And in Seattle’s Gas Works Park, a major, creative overhaul included converting a former boiler house into a picnic shelter.
In the 1990s, the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area was created in eight counties in Southwestern Pennsylvania around Pittsburgh. Last year, a record number of people toured the area’s four industrial sites, a spokesperson told me via email. The Rivers experience highlights the steel industry and also showcases historic graffiti and the work of guerrilla artists, who built sculptures in the abandoned structures during the era of abandonment. The impact of industry on the environment is also a focus.
In Dayton, Ohio, the Wright Co. Airplane factory, built in 1910 for flight pioneers Wilbur and Orville Wright, is now part of the National Aviation Heritage Area. Monthly tours are offered while the property remains under negotiation and restoration.
The Aviation Area’s website includes a video statement from David McCullough, the Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and author of “The Wright Brothers.” In the video, McCullough describes the importance of preserving manufacturing history.
Industrial structures are being reimagined as art galleries, event spaces, museums and parks. They’re also being preserved as tourism sites that highlight early manufacturing. Here are some to consider.
Carrie Furnaces, Rankin, Pa.: Part of the Rivers of Steel National Heritage area, it includes a blast-furnace tour of the iron-making process that drove the Pittsburgh-area economy.
Gas Works Park, Seattle: A former coal gasification plant was reimagined as a public park and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Landscape architect Richard Haag included the existing boiler house and exhauster-compressor as iconic features.
Hopewell Furnace National Historic Site, Elverson, Pa.: This 848-acre site includes restored structures that were part of an iron plantation. The nearly self-sufficient community, a forerunner to company towns, operated from 1771 to 1883.
Inglis Grain Elevators National Historic Site, Inglis, Manitoba: Circa-1920s slope-shouldered wooden grain elevators, dubbed the five prairie giants, represent the golden era of Western Canada’s role as a global breadbasket.
Quincy Mine, Hancock, Mich.: America’s copper boom in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula is revealed through several tours. Part of the Keweenaw National Historical Park.
Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site, Saugus, Mass.: Home to working waterwheels, forges, mills and a 17th-century dwelling.
Silo City, Buffalo: Tours to the top of these grain elevators (10 stories via stairs, plus a few ladder rungs) or at ground level, illustrate how malt was made from barley.

71b02a23-5d23-4c8d-952d-ae7f37b1408e.content:
Speaker assistant says: Organizing a fundraising event for a local animal shelter can be a challenging task, but with strategic planning and execution, it can be a great success. Here is a comprehensive plan for organizing a fundraising event to support a local animal shelter:

Step 1: Determine fundraising goals and objectives

The first step in organizing a fundraising event for a local animal shelter is to determine what the fundraiser's objectives are. Consider the amount of funds you would like to raise, the number of people to attend the event, and how the funds will be utilized to support the shelter. The goals and objectives will guide the entire fundraising process.

Step 2: Identify potential donors and partners

To have a successful fundraiser, you need to identify potential donors and partners who are interested in supporting the animal shelter. Potential donors and partners may include local businesses, animal lovers clubs, animal welfare organizations, and pet owners. Reach out to these groups and individuals to request their support in the form of donations or partnerships with the animal shelter.

Step 3: Fix a budget

Once you have identified potential donors and partners, it's time to determine the budget for the fundraising event. Setting a budget will help you determine the fundraising goals and objectives, fundraising activities, venue, marketing strategies, and other costs. Ensure the budget is realistic and reasonable based on your fundraising goals and objectives.

Step 4: Identify fundraising activities

The next step is to identify the types of fundraising activities to be implemented during the event. These fundraising activities can include silent auctions, raffle draws, bake sales, and charity runs. Research other animal welfare fundraisers to find innovative and exciting fundraising ideas that you can adapt to your event.

Step 5: Recruit volunteers

You'll need volunteers to work on the event day, ranging from setup to cleanup, customer service, and event coordination. Recruit volunteers from the animal shelter or members of the community. Schedule volunteer training sessions to ensure that everyone working on the day of the event is adequately briefed on their roles.

Step 6: Marketing strategy

Marketing your fundraising event is crucial for its success. Create a marketing plan and strategies that will help you reach and engage with the target audience. Some of the marketing tactics you can use include social media marketing, email marketing, posters and flyers, and marketing partnerships with other pet-related organizations.

Step 7: Organize the venue

The venue for the event needs to be spacious enough to accommodate the number of people you expect to attend, and it should be easy to access. You can choose a local park, community center, or an event facility to serve as the venue for your fundraising event.

In conclusion, organizing a fundraising event for a local animal shelter can be a challenging but rewarding experience. By developing a detailed plan that covers all essential elements of fundraising, including budgeting, fundraising activities, marketing strategy, volunteer recruitment, and event venue organization, you can raise essential funds to support the animal shelter's operations and improve its facilities.
71b02a23-5d23-4c8d-952d-ae7f37b1408e.context: This content provides a comprehensive seven-step guide for organizing a successful fundraising event to support a local animal shelter, covering goal setting, budgeting, activity selection, and marketing.

1. Leverage Social Media: Use social media platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram to promote the fundraiser. Create an event page and share it with your network and animal welfare groups. Use relevant hashtags, share photos of animals from the shelter, and tag local businesses and organizations.

2. Email Marketing: Send an email blast to your email list, which can include past donors, volunteers, and supporters of the shelter. Make sure to include details about the event and any exciting activities, such as live music or food trucks.

3. Flyer Distribution: Design and print flyers with details about the event and its objectives. Distribute them in high-traffic pet-friendly areas such as local parks, dog-friendly cafes, and pet stores.

4. Event Partnerships: Partner with other animal welfare organizations in the area to promote the fundraiser. They can help you spread the word to their network and will likely share the event details with their members.

5. Media Outreach: Send a press release to local media outlets such as television, radio, and newspapers. Highlight the importance of the fundraiser, its goals, and activities. It'd be best to also include a spokesperson from the animal shelter who can speak about the fundraiser and the shelter's operations.

6. Online Fundraising Platforms: Use online fundraising platforms such as GoFundMe or Kickstarter. Create a campaign that highlights the event's objectives and activities and share it on social media and in email communications.

Remember, the key to effective marketing is to choose the right channels that reach your target audience, be creative, and communicate a clear message about the importance of animal welfare and the animal shelter's fundraising objectives.

Speaker assistant says: Absolutely! Here are some tips to attract more donors and generate more donations during the fundraising event:

1. Provide Multiple Ways to Donate: Make the donation process as easy and convenient as possible. Set up several donation stations or provide a link to donate online. Accept various forms of payment, such as cash, credit card, or mobile payment methods.

2. Offer Incentives for Donations: Encourage attendees to donate by offering incentives, such as a chance to win a prize or participate in an auction. Consider offering tiered levels of rewards for larger donations.

3. Sell Merchandise: Sell branded merchandise such as t-shirts, mugs, or keychains with the animal shelter's logo. The merchandise not only generates additional funds, but also increases visibility and awareness of the shelter's cause.

Speaker assistant says: Katie had always been a highly successful businesswoman. She was intelligent, ambitious, and goal-driven. These qualities had helped her climb the corporate ladder quickly, but as a result, they had left little room for empathy. Her colleagues often accused her of being cold and ruthless in her decision-making. In her personal life, she wasn't much different. Katie was too busy with work to form any deep relationships, let alone care about the struggles of others.

One day, while on her lunch break, Katie stumbled upon a homeless shelter. Curiosity getting the best of her, she decided to step inside. The atmosphere was sullen and uninviting, and the people around her seemed downtrodden and hopeless. Katie felt a pang in her chest but quickly brushed it off, reminding herself that she had no time for such emotions.

Despite this initial resistance, Katie couldn't shake the image of the shelter from her mind. She found herself thinking about the homeless people she had seen there, wondering what their lives were like before they ended up on the streets. Slowly but surely, the idea of volunteering at the shelter began to take shape in her mind. It was a spur of the moment decision - Katie surprised even herself by signing up for a shift the very next day.

The experience was eye-opening for Katie. She quickly realized how easy it is to slip through the cracks and end up homeless. Some volunteers tried to give the shelter's residents some life advice or soothing words, but Katie found such conversations awkward and repetitive. She decided to take a different approach. Instead of telling them what to do or say, she started listening to them intently.

The first couple of weeks of volunteering were difficult for Katie. She had to face a lot of harsh realities like having to turn people away because of a lack of space or resources. She had never experienced such poverty and hopelessness up close before, and it made her feel somewhat helpless. However, as she continued to consistently show up at the shelter every week, she began to build relationships with the people living there. They trusted her to listen to them, and as a result, Katie began to understand their daily struggles.

It wasn't long before Katie realized how much her actions could affect the other people around her. By showing people empathy and listening to their concerns, she could make a real difference in their lives. It was an incredibly powerful feeling. She started to volunteer more often and became more proactive with her efforts. For the first time in her life, Katie felt passionate about something other than her work.

Katie's new role at the shelter soon began to change her outside of it. Her interactions with the people who visited the shelter made her more compassionate and aware of others' needs. She started to take a more thoughtful approach to her business decisions, considering how they would affect those around her. These small changes in behavior gradually turned into more profound, long-term changes. Katie's friends and colleagues started to notice how much more approachable and empathetic she had become.

The experience eventually came full circle when a homeless man approached her on the street one day, recognizing her from her volunteer work. He thanked her for her kindness and compassion, telling her that her efforts had made a significant difference in his life. Katie felt a wave of emotion overtake her as she connected with someone whose life had been transformed by her actions. In that moment, Katie knew that her time at the shelter had given her a new sense of purpose.

From that day forward, Katie made sure that volunteering at the shelter became a permanent fixture in her life. It was no longer a brief moment of curiosity but an integral part of who she was. Katie had transformed from a person who only cared about herself to someone who felt a deep sense of empathy for others. Though it had taken her time to get there, she finally understood that small acts of kindness and a listening ear could make a profound difference in someone else's life.

The Craven County Disaster Recovery Alliance (CCDRA) - a long-term recovery group (LTRG) began meeting soon after Hurricane Matthew hit eastern NC in October 2016. The LTRG was formed with the help of FEMA Volunteer Agency Liaisons and a coalition comprised of representatives from corporations, faith based organizations, community non-profits, governmental agencies, and concerned citizens in January 2017.
CCDRA's vision is to continue assisting those still affected from Hurricane Matthew with long-term recovery and unmet needs assistance and to be an ongoing resource for all future disasters that will happen again in Craven County.
In June 2018, the CCDRA team of volunteers is organizing a Disaster Preparedness Workshop for churches and non-profits. This is the first step to help prepare our community for a disaster. This website has been created to help the community be better prepared when a disaster happens and to better educate families, businesses, groups and those who are eventually affected by a disaster on what to do next. Long-term recovery is a long process, sometimes 2+ years after the actual disaster, but if you know what to do before or immediately after a disaster the better off all those affected will be.
CCDRA will be working with organizations in our county to form a Community Organization Active in Disaster (COAD). The Craven County COAD will consist of representatives from public, private and not-for-profit agencies whose goal will be to share information and resources that will help residents prepare for, respond to and recover from future disasters.
